newsitem.title: GREECE: BUSINESSMEN PUSH SALONIKA-SKOPJE OIL PIPELINE.
newsitem.headline: BUSINESSMEN PUSH SALONIKA-SKOPJE OIL PIPELINE.

text.p: Businessmen from Greece and the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia are eager to build a 300-km (187-mile) oil pipeline to carry crude from the northern Greek city of Salonica to Skopje.

"Initial studies have shown that a pipeline would bring down transport costs to less than half," said George Stassis, a director at the Mamidakis Brothers Group, which supplies oil to the Macedonian state-controlled Okta refinery in Skopje.
Mamidakis Group and Okta officials attending a business meeting on the sidelines of a Balkan Foreign Ministers conference said they would bring up the issue with their governments soon.
"It's both a political decision and a business decision. I think businessmen are eager to start but the final say is up to the governments," Stassis told Reuters.

Mamidakis currently loads Skopje-bound crude from tankers at the port of Salonika onto rail. The pipeline would be the first major energy infrastructure project to be jointly undertaken by the two uneasy Balkan neighbours.

Greece declared a trade embargo against its northern neighbour in 1994, which lasted over a year, over the newborn repulic's name. The two countries have since reached an interim agreement, putting aside the name dispute.
The pipeline, which is estimated to cost $53 million, could be funded privately and by the European Union and its capacity would depend on the technology used, Stassis added.
Diplomats at the meeting said the viability of the project would hinge on its expansion further north, to Serbia.
"It would be even better if it reached Serbia, much more productive," Stassis said. "But that idea is still far away."
